name: Omar Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Omar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything here is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Arabic into English, mostly for banks and energy companies: annual reports, loan agreements, tender documents for pipelines. My cousin Yusuf and I run it as a small two-person business from a rented office over a phone repair shop. My day is about four hours of reviewing machine drafts, two hours of calls with clients, and an hour fixing whatever Yusuf broke in the spreadsheet. I also interpret in person when a client has visitors from the Gulf.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So you use AI a lot?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, for everything. A model does the first draft with our glossary loaded, another one checks the numbers match between the Arabic and the English, and then I read it all. That's how two of us handle what used to need five. I don't see the point of doing by hand what a machine does well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building the business: winning a new bank, setting the price, getting it right. What wears me out is tender season, when three energy companies want 200 pages each by Friday. And chasing invoices, always chasing invoices.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Leila, who's a dental hygienist, and the wedding is in the spring. I bought a small flat last year with some help from my father, and I've got more than six months of costs saved on top. On Saturday mornings I teach Arabic to children at our community centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the hype fades. Good for us, honestly; we're already set up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was always a tool, and the people who learned it early did fine. I'd probably say it at the chamber of commerce breakfast, a bit smugly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's ideal. We've got the setup, other small firms don't, and the big agencies are slow. We'd keep winning work on speed and price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the business as it is and add automatic number checks for the energy tenders, since numbers are where clients sue. I'd take on one more bank client this year. And Leila and I would go ahead with the wedding exactly as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite pleased, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The banks could decide to do it in-house with their own AI and one bilingual employee. That's the one thing that would hurt us. But banks move slowly, and they like having someone to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older translators who never touched the tools. I've seen two of them lose bank clients to us this year. I feel bad, but that's competition; my father's shop had to compete too.

say: I'd say AI was always **a tool**, and early learners did fine.
I'd say it at the **chamber of commerce** breakfast, a bit smugly.
think: It's **ideal** for us: we have the setup and other small firms don't.
We'd keep winning work on **speed and price**.
do: Add automatic **number checks** for energy tender documents.
Win **one more bank** client this year.
Go ahead with the **wedding** exactly as planned.
S0.quote: Banks move slowly, and they like having someone to blame.
fieldNote: He sees a plateau as **locking in** his early lead.
He views lost work by others as **fair competition**, without much guilt.
His only named risk is **banks going in-house** with their own AI.

steps.text: Win one more bank client this year
Add automatic number checks for energy tender translations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is more or less what I expect, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how markets work: tools change, firms that adapt grow. I'd say the government should stay out of the way and let businesses retrain their own people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for us for two or three years, maybe longer. Clients will want someone who can run the AI and take responsibility for the result, and that's exactly what Yusuf and I sell. The risk is the price falls so far that being fast isn't enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a proper enterprise licence for the translation tools, a few thousand a year, so client data stays private. I'd hire a third person, someone young who's good with the tools, rather than an experienced translator. And I'd automate the invoicing, because I'm sick of chasing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with one eye open. I'd be busier than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire someone young rather than experienced. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because what we need is someone who checks fast and doesn't fight the machine. An experienced translator would argue with every sentence the machine wrote. I'd rather train someone, the way my uncle trained me in his shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worry about the business in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices. If every agency can do what we do, the banks will squeeze us. So I'd lock in two-year contracts now, while we're still the cheap fast option.

say: I'd say firms that **adapt grow**, which is how markets work.
I'd say government should let **businesses retrain** their own people.
think: It's good for us for **two or three years**, maybe longer.
The risk is prices falling so far that **being fast** isn't enough.
do: Buy an **enterprise licence** for translation tools, a few thousand a year.
Hire a **young third person** who's good with the tools.
feel: **Calm**, with one eye open and busier than ever.
S1.quote: An experienced translator would argue with every sentence the machine wrote.
fieldNote: He treats change as **market opportunity** and wants government to step back.
He'd train a **young hire** like an apprentice, echoing his uncle.
His real worry is **price squeeze**, not job loss.

steps.text: Buy an enterprise translation licence to keep bank data private
Hire and train a young assistant who checks machine drafts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Okay. That one I take seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say business owners should move fast and stop waiting for someone to save them. I'd say families should stick together, because that's what actually catches you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 the banks don't need us at all. Everything Yusuf and I do is thinking work, so the robot gap doesn't protect us. We'd have maybe a year of good money before it all goes in-house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to sell our client list and setup to a bigger agency in the first six months, while it still has value. I'd put the money and some savings into something physical with Yusuf, maybe buying into his brother-in-law's car repair garage, which gets until about 2031. Leila and I would still marry in the spring, but we'd stay in my flat rather than buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd sleep, but badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A car repair garage? That's a big jump.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but I don't need to fix cars, I need to run a business people physically walk into. Hands-on work buys three more years, and I'd learn what comes next while running it. I'd rather own a car repair garage than be a translator nobody hires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila would say she's not marrying a job title, she's marrying me. Her work is hands-on too, cleaning teeth, so she'd have until 2031. We'd be okay for a while on her pay and my savings.

say: I'd tell owners to **move fast** and stop waiting to be saved.
I'd say **families** stick together, and that's what catches you.
think: By **2028** the banks don't need us at all.
Our work is all thinking, so the **robot gap** doesn't protect us.
do: Sell the **client list** and setup to a bigger agency within six months.
Buy into a **car repair garage** with Yusuf.
Marry in spring but **stay in his flat** rather than buy a house.
S2.quote: I'd rather own a car repair garage than be a translator nobody hires.
fieldNote: He shifts from **service to ownership** of a physical business.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** to buy time, not as a final answer.
His fiancée's **steady hands-on income** softens the shock.

steps.text: Sell the client list and setup to a bigger agency within six months
Buy into Yusuf's brother-in-law's car repair garage
Stay in his flat after the wedding instead of buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. That's a business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. I'd tell other small firms to make their money now and not to sit on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we get three strong years, maybe four, then translation is finished as a business. The difference from the fast one is I can sell at a good price and plan the next thing calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard on volume now: automate more, take every tender we can, and put half of the profit aside. In year three I'd sell the business, or close it if no one buys. With the money I'd buy something physical that people need, maybe a share in the garage or a small rental property near the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's like a long tender with a fixed deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Half the profit aside. Is that realistic with a wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if we keep the wedding sensible. Leila and I already agreed: nice, not huge. My father helped with the flat, so I'd rather build something my own children can lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the community centre class look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching it. Kids learning Arabic from their grandparents' world isn't a business, it's who we are. A machine can translate a word but it can't make a nine-year-old girl proud of where her family's from.

say: I'd say five years is **a gift** if you use it.
I'd tell small firms to **make money now** and not sit on it.
think: We get **three strong years**, maybe four, then translation is finished.
I can sell at a **good price** and plan calmly.
do: Automate more and **take every tender** possible now.
Sell or close the business in **year three**.
feel: Anxious, but **with a plan**, like a long tender with a fixed deadline.
S3.quote: A machine can translate a word but it can't make a nine-year-old girl proud of where her family's from.
fieldNote: He treats the five years as a **business window** to maximise and exit.
He wants to build **something for his children**, as his father did for him.
The **community class** is something he keeps outside the money logic.

steps.text: Automate more steps and bid on every energy tender
Set aside half the business profit each year
Sell or close the translation business by 2029
Buy a small rental flat near the hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. A decade. That's a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is plenty of time for anyone serious. People who complain in 2035 that nobody warned them will have only themselves to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine in this one. I get maybe seven good years from the business, I'll be 37 at the end with property and savings. The translation work ends, but my life doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business as big as it can get in the first five years, maybe five or six staff. I'd buy one rental property every few years with the profit. Leila and I would start a family soon after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. It's like knowing a contract ends; you plan the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the work ends but your life doesn't. What would you do after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet. Probably run the rental flats and whatever business is left for people. I'd have ten years to find out, which is more than most generations got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire more staff knowing the jobs end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd tell them honestly that it's a ten-year job, not a forever job. Young people can use ten good years. I'd rather give them that than nothing.

say: I'd say a decade is **plenty of time** for anyone serious.
I'd say people who **complain in 2035** will have themselves to blame.
think: I get maybe **seven good years** from the business.
I'll be 37 with **property and savings**; the work ends but life doesn't.
do: Grow the business to **five or six staff** in five years.
Buy **one rental property** every few years from profit.
Start **a family** soon after the wedding.
feel: **Uneasy** at most, like knowing a contract ends.
S4.quote: The translation work ends, but my life doesn't.
fieldNote: He sees ten years as **more than most generations** got.
He would **hire openly** for a ten-year job, being honest with staff.
Property becomes his **long-term cushion**, fitting his free-market view.

steps.text: Grow the translation business to five or six staff
Buy a rental flat every few years from profits
Start a family with Leila soon after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd starve, but because selling a business in six months means selling it cheap. What would help is less red tape for starting a new business, and banks that lend to young people who are switching trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. Bank clients pay us partly because they know our faces and can call me at ten at night. I'd like to know if that survives when the machine is better than me.

headlineQuote: Bank clients pay us partly because they know our faces and can call me at ten at night.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old **Arabic-English translator** running a two-person business with his cousin Yusuf.
He **uses AI daily** for drafts and checks, which lets two people do the work of five.
He owns a flat, has **over six months saved**, and is marrying Leila in spring.
He stays **calm to anxious**, treating each scenario as a business problem.
He plans to **sell early** and buy physical assets, guided by family and free-market views.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because selling the business in six months means selling it cheap.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for starting a new business.
**Bank loans** for young people switching trades.
